Definition: Extent to which the data exchange enables services accessible to all population groups including persons with disabilities, elderly, low literacy
Comments: Internet penetration 30.5% (2023, ITU). Mobile phone penetration 55%. Around 40 million people do not use mobile internet (GSMA). 2G/3G/4G cover 75%/55%/45% of population. Significant digital exclusion. No specific accessibility standards documented for e-government services.
revision_notes: Original source (Ecofin Agency article on data centre investment talks) does not actually address accessibility for persons with disabilities, the elderly or low-literacy users; it was only tangentially relevant. Fetched G3ict's Digital Accessibility Rights Evaluation (DARE) Index for DRC, which is a directly authoritative source on ICT accessibility: it confirms a general disability-rights law exists but there is no legal definition of ICT accessibility, no reasonable-accommodation definition, no universal service obligation covering persons with disabilities, and no formal mechanism for disabled persons' organisations to shape ICT policy. Cross-checked internet/mobile exclusion figures against DataReportal's Digital 2026 DRC report (30.5% internet penetration, ~79 million offline). Combined evidence supports the existing score of 1 (Limited accessibility); confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: DR Congo's data exchange offers limited accessibility to persons with disabilities, the elderly and low-literacy users. Internet penetration stands at 30.5% of the population and around 79 million people remain offline (DataReportal, Digital 2026 DRC report); GSMA estimates some 40 million people are not connected to mobile internet. G3ict's Digital Accessibility Rights Evaluation Index records that DRC has a general law protecting the rights of persons with disabilities but no legal definition of ICT accessibility, no reasonable-accommodation requirement, no universal service obligation extending to persons with disabilities, and no established process for involving disabled persons' organisations in ICT accessibility policymaking. No accessibility standards are documented for e-government services specifically.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government data exchange systems. 25 variables in 4 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether data exchange infrastructure and services reach rural and remote areas or concentrate in urban centers
Comments: Severe urban-rural digital divide. Only 5,150 telecom towers for a country of 905,000 sq miles and 112M people. PNN2 targets 30,000 towers by 2030. 4G coverage only 45% of population. GSMA estimates 40M Congolese did not use mobile internet in 2023. Digital services highly concentrated in Kinshasa.
revision_notes: Both originally cited sources (Tech in Africa on the €8B digital plan, Ecofin Agency on data centre talks) are relevant background but only indirectly evidence the urban-rural divide itself. Verified and refreshed with a British International Investment-commissioned fibre impact study (using 2024 World Bank/GSMA data showing urban internet penetration of ~38% versus ~25% in rural areas), a May 2026 Connecting Africa piece confirming 3G/4G coverage at 68%/57% with rural connectivity still a major gap, and a February 2026 Bankable Africa report on DRC's new ten-year (2026-2035) FDSU infrastructure-sharing strategy targeting the roughly 68 million people still living in unconnected rural areas. This evidence confirms the divide remains severe and largely unaddressed at present, supporting the existing score of 1 (Primarily urban); confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: Digital infrastructure and services in DR Congo remain heavily concentrated in urban centres, above all Kinshasa. As of 2024, 2G/3G/4G networks covered roughly 75%/68%/57% of the population respectively, but rural areas lag well behind urban ones: internet penetration is estimated at around 38% in urban areas against approximately 25% in rural areas (World Bank/GSMA data cited in a 2025 British International Investment fibre-impact study). The country's Universal Service Development Fund (FDSU) has launched a ten-year (2026-2035) infrastructure-sharing strategy explicitly to extend coverage to the roughly 68 million people living in rural areas, and government plans call for expanding telecom towers from 5,150 to 30,000 by 2030 and connecting 650 additional communities. These initiatives are only just beginning, so data exchange infrastructure and services remain primarily urban for now.
